prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices can amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B040, credited to Kiyotaki and Moore. Having read the exchange, I rank the common criteria as follows. First comes clarity of attribution. Second is conceptual generality: a single mechanism, in which borrowing limits tied to collateral feed back on asset prices, now organises how a large body of macro-finance and policy modelling treats financial frictions. Third is maturity measured in elapsed time. The 1997 contribution has had nearly three decades of extension, critique and use, including after 2008. No other shortlisted candidate combines a two-person originating claim with that track record, and the three-name cap forces no arbitrary cut. I have sharpened one thing. The citation should recognise the mechanism and its influence on how credit cycles and crises are modelled. It should not imply that the size of the amplification is empirically settled. The Dreber-Almenberg and Strömberg wording points the same way, and I adopt it. Support counts are not merit. Scientific arguments did move me on one point: B044 is stronger than my round-1 rank of eighth implied, and I now treat it as my principal alternative.
statement.case_against: The reservations I stated in round 1 remain. (1) Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. I think the mechanisms are distinct, but that view comes from general knowledge and the exchange, and I have not verified it here. (2) Direct empirical validation of the amplification mechanism is more indirect and mixed than the theory's influence suggests, which is a real weakness for a prize resting essentially on one seminal paper and its extensions. (3) Excluding Gertler and Gilchrist leaves out the more empirical and quantitative strand and honours theory over tested evidence. Dreber-Almenberg is right that the Committee should say so openly. If members who know the macro-finance literature show that the 2022 recognition leaves little marginal room, or that the quantitative-validation gap is wider than I assume, my case would weaken considerably. B044 would then become my first choice, provided its citation is anchored on the trade-shock evidence.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B044 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, moved from his opening pair because the China-shock design is a three-author product. He argues that a decade of refinement without overturning the core finding is the relevant test of maturity, and that the citation should rest on empirical evidence about trade and technology exposure, not on a unified task theory. He answered my recency and identification concerns directly.
responses.response: I accept the substance. His move to the trio resolves the attribution problem I raised: leaving Dorn out of a three-author design would be indefensible, and I would support him in the trio if B044 advanced. His maturity argument has force, since refinement of the magnitudes without loss of the qualitative result is a fair test after about ten years. What he does not answer for me is the difference in kind between the two candidates. B044 is a credibly identified body of evidence with an acknowledged inference debate. B040 is a general mechanism whose originating claim has been scrutinised for almost three decades. On clarity and durability I still put B040 slightly ahead, but I now see the gap as narrow and not as the eighth-versus-first difference of my opening ranking. If the citation is anchored on trade-shock evidence alone, as he and Krusell propose, my hesitation about B044 shrinks. That bears on the chair's question about a narrower citation.

responses.point: Krusell moved from B002 to B044 on maturity grounds. He would anchor the citation on trade-shock evidence, where credit for Autor, Dorn and Hanson is clean, and he describes B040's empirical validation as more indirect, with the 2022 prize narrowing its marginal novelty.
responses.response: I agree with him on B002 and have not been moved to put it in my configuration. His concern about indirect validation is one I list myself. I would separate two things, though. How much amplification collateral constraints contribute quantitatively in a given model is contested. The conceptual claim that collateral values and asset prices create a feedback loop has nonetheless been absorbed across macro, corporate finance and policy analysis. Even so, the overlap point is the one most likely to change my view. I would like to hear which specific features of Kiyotaki-Moore he thinks the 2022 recognition already covers. My understanding is that it covered bank runs, deposit insurance and the study of bank failures. Collateral-driven asset-price feedback in the real economy is a different mechanism. I have not verified that, and I would revise if he shows otherwise.

responses.point: Friberg keeps B024 first with Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn, argues that BLP is a substantive advance that made markups, welfare and merger effects measurable, and rejects the idea that a clean mechanism ranks above an empirical framework just because it is simpler to state. He now lists B040 as a close alternative.
responses.response: I agree on the criterion he names, what the contribution changed in practice and how long it has lasted, and on that criterion I rank B024 second among my alternatives. The BLP trio is a more compact core than the seven-name credited set suggests, and limiting the citation to demand estimation with endogenous prices is a sound way to handle Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. My remaining hesitation is the one I raised in round 1. A methods contribution depends on functional-form and instrument assumptions, so its credibility varies across applications. I also think B040's attribution is cleaner, since no obvious co-originator sits outside its credited pair. He is right that I should not favour B040 just because it is easier to state. My reason for placing B040 first is originating clarity, not simplicity. I keep B024 as an alternative and would not oppose it on merit.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg supports B040 with the same pair. She calls the lack of direct empirical validation the most serious reservation, wants the citation drafted around the mechanism and its influence, and wants the Committee to say openly that excluding Gertler and Gilchrist favours theory over tested evidence.
responses.response: I agree and have adopted her drafting approach. The citation now says that collateral constraints and asset prices "can" amplify and propagate shocks, which claims the mechanism and not a measured magnitude. I also accept her second point. The pair-only credit is justified by the independent origin of the collateral-constraint mechanism and the cleanness of the originating paper, not by prior recognition of the accelerator. The cost to Gertler and Gilchrist is real, and the Committee should record it. I would not widen the credit to cover that cost, because adding names would blur the attribution that I regard as this candidate's main strength.

responses.point: The chair supports B040 with the two originators and considered adding Autor as a second part, but decided that a one-name part would misrepresent the China-shock work. He keeps B044 as a first alternative on scientific strength and says that he would revisit his choice if the exclusion of Dorn were resolved.
responses.response: I agree that a multi-part configuration is not viable here. B040 plus a B044 part would need at least two names for the second part, and a B040 pair plus Autor, Dorn and Hanson would total five people, exceeding the cap. Splitting B044 would also misattribute a joint design. That answers the chair's question for me: I would consider only single-part configurations. I also see the chair's remark that B044 weakens as a reservation if the Committee decides the trade-shock evidence is the achievement. I think the Committee needs to settle that scope question before it settles names, and I would back the narrower citation if B044 is chosen. I disclose that the chair and I both rank B040 first, so our agreement is not independent evidence.

uncertainties: Whether the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises narrows the marginal case for Kiyotaki and Moore enough to change the ordering. I rely on general knowledge and the exchange, not independent verification.

How much weight indirect or mixed empirical validation should carry against conceptual generality and demonstrated influence, and whether the Committee prefers a mechanism or a credibly identified body of evidence this year.

Whether a B044 citation anchored on trade-shock evidence and local labour markets, with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, would be judged a single mature achievement. About a decade of replication may or may not be enough, and shift-share inference remains debated.
Whether adding Gertler or Gilchrist would improve the credit by covering the empirical and quantitative strand, or would blur an otherwise clean attribution.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied materials, and I have not independently verified citation counts, replication records or the scope of earlier prizes.
statement.conflict_note: Updated, with no new disclosures. The supplied profile lists no co-authorship, institutional or collaborative tie to Kiyotaki or Moore, to the B044 names (Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz), or to the B024 names (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn and the others). My research is in market and mechanism design (matching, auctions, fair allocation) and my first-ranked candidate lies outside that field. My Lund co-authors and refugee-matching and kidney-exchange collaborators are not credited on any shortlisted candidate. I am an SSE affiliate alongside committee colleagues Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg, which is an institutional connection and not a tie to any candidate. I also gave the 2020 presentation speech, which reflected the Academy and does not establish a personal preference now. I note that the chair and I both support B040, and I disclose this without adjudicating it.
